text: Context Language Models (CLMs) are introduced by their authors as a way for models to manage their own context, implemented by treating the context as a file the model may update without restriction.

The motivation is consistent across sources: serving is shifting toward long-context applications, prefill cost grows rapidly with input length, and agents on repository-level software engineering face accumulating history against bounded context windows.

Exact prefix reuse is confined to contexts sharing a prefix verbatim, and standard prefix-cache reuse must re-prefill everything after the first mismatch. Suffix Cache Reuse (SCR) reuses the cached states of surviving tokens after an edit and re-prefills only newly inserted or appended tokens.

SCR reuses cached states of all surviving tokens after an edit and re-prefills only new or appended tokens. The price is stale states encoding the previous prefix, which the authors say can sometimes be beneficial; the claims give no general quality guarantee.

Reuse outside a shared prefix is not free in general: another source notes that non-prefix KV reuse breaks cross-chunk attention and significantly degrades generation quality. This pulls against treating CLM's stale-state reuse as unproblematic.

The RLM evidence is of a different kind. Its authors report handling inputs two orders of magnitude beyond context windows and outperforming compaction, CodeAct with sub-calls and Claude Code across four long-context tasks at comparable cost. The claims do not say these tasks are coding workloads.
A reproduction found that deeper recursion, or use on simple retrieval, hurts performance and inflates time and tokens. This qualifies the original cost claim, since the original left depth at one.

For CLM, the claims establish authors' reports of 11.4% higher accuracy with 21.5% fewer prefix-reuse FLOPs on BrowseComp-Plus, parity on TerminalBench 2.1 with 29.5% fewer FLOPs, and 35% less server-side compute than standard SGLang at matched performance.

The CLM paper includes recursive language models as baselines on a shared Mini-SWE-Agent backbone, so an RLM-versus-CLM comparison exists in it. The CLM headline results are reported in FLOPs, and they come from the CLM authors themselves.
